hero.title: Learn words with the words they go with
hero.lead: Short units on collocations and academic vocabulary for IELTS and university. Test yourself, notice the words in a real text, work out the patterns, practise, then see how much you’ve improved. No sign-in.

A2.name: Elementary
A2.cando: Everyday study words and their partners.
A2.about: You can talk about familiar topics in simple sentences.

B1.name: Intermediate
B1.cando: Common collocations for essays and graphs.
B1.about: You can describe experiences and processes and give simple reasons and opinions.

B2.name: Upper-intermediate
B2.about: You can write clear, connected texts and explain a viewpoint. A typical level for starting university.

C1.name: Advanced
C1.cando: Precise language for sources and evidence.
C1.about: You can write well-structured, detailed academic texts and use language flexibly.

A2: Linking words: and, but, because, so

related.d: Short practice for a more academic style
Practise reporting verbs and in-text citations

units.title: Study life collocations
units.cando: Talk about classes, assignments and exams with natural word partners.

words.m: write down key points while you listen or read
words.ex: I always take notes in lectures.
All students must attend the first lecture.

words.m: give your work to the teacher
words.ex: Please hand in your assignment by Friday.
I worked all weekend to meet the deadline.
If you miss the deadline, you lose marks.

words.m: take an exam (British and Australian English)
words.ex: We sit the final exam in June.

words.m: get / not get the mark you need
words.ex: She passed all her exams.

words.m: study your notes again before a test
words.ex: I’m revising for my exam this weekend.

pre.q: Please ___ notes during the lecture.
I need to ___ my assignment by Friday.
She worked all night to ___ the deadline.

pre.instr: Type the missing word. It means ‘study again before a test’.
pre.q: I’m ___ for my exam this weekend, so I can’t go out.
All first-year students must ___ the welcome lecture.

notice.title: A message to a classmate
notice.instr: Read the message. Tap every verb + noun partner about studying (like do homework).
notice.text: Hi Ali, are you going to [[attend the lecture]] tomorrow? I was sick last week, so I couldn’t [[take notes]]. I also need to [[hand in my assignment]] by Friday. I don’t want to [[miss the deadline]] again! After that, I’ll [[revise for the exam]]. We [[sit the exam]] on the 20th. Wish me luck! Ben
notice.after: Each noun has its own verb partner: take notes, miss a deadline. Could you change the verbs? You’ll find out next.

discover.ctx: take notes · hand in my assignment · attend the lecture
discover.q: We say ‘take notes’. Which one is NOT natural?
discover.hint: Which verb never goes with notes?
discover.insight: We take notes (in a lecture) or make notes (from a book). We don’t ‘do’ notes.

discover.ctx: meet the deadline · miss the deadline
discover.q: What is the opposite of ‘meet a deadline’?
discover.hint: Look at Ben’s message.
discover.insight: meet a deadline = finish on time; miss a deadline = finish late. Also: extend a deadline = give more time.

discover.ctx: sit the exam · revise for the exam
discover.q: In Australia and the UK, what does ‘revise for an exam’ mean?
o: Study your notes again before the exam
discover.hint: Ben does this after he hands in his assignment, before the exam.
discover.insight: revise = study again before a test (American English: review). sit an exam = take an exam.

rule.title: Your word card
points: Learn nouns with their verb partners: take notes, meet a deadline, sit an exam.
The verb usually can’t be changed: <s>do notes</s>, <s>win a deadline</s>.
rule.watch: assist = help. To go to a lecture is attend: assist a lecture → attend a lecture.

practice.instr: Match each verb with its partner.

practice.q: Oh no! I ___ the deadline. Can I still submit it?
practice.hint: The opposite of meet a deadline.
practice.why: miss a deadline = be too late.

practice.q: I always ___ notes on my laptop in lectures.
Which one is NOT natural?
practice.hint: You can win a game, but not…
practice.why: pass / fail / sit an exam. We don’t ‘win’ an exam.
Go to a lecture = attend a lecture.

practice.a: You must hand in the assignment by Monday.
practice.why: hand in + the assignment + by + day.

post.q: Don’t forget to ___ notes in the seminar.
When do we have to ___ the essay?
post.why: hand in = give your work to the teacher. (hand out = give to everyone, e.g. worksheets.)

post.q: If you ___ the deadline, you lose 5% per day.
We ___ the final exam in the main hall next Tuesday.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences about your study routine or your next exam. Use at least four collocations from this unit.
produce.target: study collocations: take notes, attend a lecture, hand in an assignment, meet/miss a deadline, sit an exam, revise for an exam
checklist: I used the right verb with each noun (take notes, meet a deadline…).
I used at least four collocations.
My sentences are about my real study life.
produce.model: I attend three lectures a week and I always take notes on my laptop. Next week, I have to hand in my first assignment. I want to meet the deadline, so I’m starting early. In June, I’ll sit two exams, so I’ll revise for them in May.

units.title: Make, do, take or have?
units.cando: Choose the right verb in common collocations: make progress, do research, take part…

words.ex: I need to make a decision about my major.
You have made great progress this term.
Everyone makes mistakes when learning.

words.m: study a topic to find information
words.ex: I did some research for my essay.

words.m: complete work set by the teacher
words.ex: I do my homework every evening.
Thirty students took part in the study.

words.m: stop and rest for a short time
words.ex: Let’s take a ten-minute break.
We had a long discussion about the topic.

pre.q: I need to ___ a decision about my course.
Many students ___ research in the library.
Would you like to ___ part in our study?

pre.s: Everyone {does} mistakes when learning a language.

pre.q: Let’s ___ a short break and continue in ten minutes.

notice.title: Feedback from a teacher
notice.instr: Read the feedback. Tap every phrase with make, do, take or have + a noun.
notice.text: You have [[made good progress]] this term. Your essay shows that you [[did a lot of research]], and you [[made very few mistakes]]. You also [[took part]] in every class discussion. Next term, try to [[take a short break]] every hour when you study, and [[do your homework]] on time. You need to [[make a decision]] about your final project soon. Let’s [[have a meeting]] next week to talk about it.
notice.after: When do we use make, and when do we use do? There is a pattern. You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: made progress · made mistakes · make a decision
discover.q: Which idea fits make best?
o: Doing a task or a job
discover.hint: A decision, progress and a mistake are all results.
discover.insight: make: creating or producing something: make a decision, make progress, make a mistake, make a plan.

discover.ctx: did research · do your homework
discover.q: Which idea fits do best?
discover.hint: Research and homework are kinds of work.
discover.insight: do: work, tasks and activities: do research, do homework, do an exercise, do a course.

discover.ctx: took part · take a break · have a meeting
discover.q: Take and have are used in fixed phrases. Which phrase is correct?
discover.hint: Look at the teacher’s feedback.
discover.insight: Some collocations just need to be learned: take part, take a break, have a meeting, have a discussion.

rule.title: Your word card
points: make = create or produce (a decision, progress, a mistake, a plan, an effort).
do = work, tasks, activities (research, homework, a course, an exercise).
take / have = fixed phrases (take part, take a break, have a meeting, have a discussion).
rule.watch: <s>do a mistake</s> → make a mistake; <s>make research</s> → do research.

practice.instr: Which verb goes with each noun?
chips: take a break / have a break

practice.q: You’ve ___ a lot of progress this year!
Have you ___ your homework?

practice.s: I {made} some research on climate change for my essay.

practice.q: How many students ___ part in the survey?

practice.a: We need to make a decision today.

post.q: It’s OK to ___ mistakes in class.
She is ___ research on online learning.
Fifty people ___ part in the interview study.

post.s: We need to {do} a decision before Friday.

post.q: Let’s ___ a meeting on Monday to plan the project.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences about your progress as a learner this year. Use at least four collocations with make, do, take or have.
produce.target: collocations with make, do, take and have
checklist: I used make for decisions, progress and mistakes.
I used do for research, homework and tasks.
I used fixed phrases like take part and take a break.
produce.model: This year I have made good progress with my writing. I do my homework every evening and I try to take a short break every hour. I took part in a speaking club, and I made a decision to do a short research course next term.

units.title: Describing trends and changes
units.cando: Describe graphs and changes: rise sharply, a slight fall, remain stable.

words.ex: Prices rose by 10%.
Sales fell in March.
The figure remained stable for two years.
Temperatures fluctuated all week.
Visitor numbers reached a peak of 9,000 in July.

words.m: by a lot, or very quickly
words.ex: Costs increased sharply.
Numbers fell slightly.
The population grew steadily.

pre.q: The number of students ___ from 200 to 500.
Sales fell ___, from 90 to 88.
Prices ___ stable between 2020 and 2022.

pre.s: There was a {sharply} increase in house prices.

pre.q: The price of oil went up and down all year: it ___ a lot.

notice.title: IELTS-style graph description
notice.instr: Read the description. Tap the words and phrases that describe how the numbers changed.
notice.text: The graph shows the number of international students at a university from 2015 to 2024. In 2015, there were about 2,000 students. The number [[rose steadily]] until 2019, when it [[reached a peak]] of 4,500. In 2020, there was [[a sharp fall]] to 2,500. The figure [[remained stable]] for the next two years and then [[increased gradually]] to 3,800 in 2024. Overall, student numbers [[fluctuated]], but they ended higher than at the start.
notice.after: Look at rose steadily and a sharp fall. They follow two different patterns. You’ll work them out next.

discover.ctx: The number rose steadily. · There was a sharp fall.
discover.q: What follows rose, and what comes before fall?
o: rose + adverb (steadily); a + adjective + noun (a sharp fall)
discover.hint: Is fall a verb or a noun here?
discover.insight: Two patterns: verb + adverb (rose steadily, fell sharply) or a/an + adjective + noun (a steady rise, a sharp fall).

discover.ctx: reached a peak of 4,500 · remained stable · fluctuated
discover.q: Which phrase means ‘stayed the same’?
discover.hint: What happened in 2021 and 2022?
discover.insight: remain stable = stay the same; fluctuate = go up and down; reach a peak = get to the highest point.

discover.ctx: slight · gradual · steady · sharp · dramatic
discover.q: Which words describe a BIG or fast change?
discover.hint: 4,500 to 2,500 in one year was ‘a … fall’.
discover.insight: Size and speed: slight (small) → gradual / steady (slow) → significant → sharp / dramatic (big or fast).

rule.title: Your word card
points: Up: rise, increase, grow. Down: fall, decrease, decline, drop. Same: remain stable. Up and down: fluctuate.
Verb + adverb: rose sharply, fell slightly.
a/an + adjective + noun: a sharp rise, a slight fall.
Highest point: reach a peak. Lowest point: hit a low.
rule.watch: raised → rose. Rise has no object (prices rose); raise needs one (they raised prices).

practice.instr: Match each word with its meaning.

practice.q: Online shopping increased ___ (dramatic) in 2020.
practice.hint: After a verb, use an adverb.

practice.q: Which describes a change from 100 to 101?

practice.s: The number of cars {raised} quickly after 2010.
practice.hint: No object: the number went up by itself.

practice.a: There was a gradual decline in sales.

practice.instr: Small or slow change, or big or fast change?

post.q: Unemployment ___ from 6% to 4%.
Sales went from 1,000 to 3,000 in one month: they rose ___.
The temperature ___ at 25°C for a week.

post.s: There was a {gradually} rise in prices.
post.why: Before a noun, use an adjective: a gradual rise.

post.q: Visitor numbers ___ a peak of 10,000 in July.

produce.task: Describe a change you know about (for example, rent in your city, or your study hours over a year). Write 3–4 sentences like an IELTS Task 1 description. Use at least three trend expressions.
produce.target: trend vocabulary: rise/fall/remain stable/fluctuate/reach a peak, with adverbs (sharply, slightly) and adjectives (a sharp rise)
checklist: I used verb + adverb (rose sharply) or a + adjective + noun (a sharp rise).
I gave numbers or dates.
I used at least three different trend words.
produce.model: Rent in my city rose steadily from 2019 to 2022, when it reached a peak of $600 a week. In 2023, there was a slight fall to $560. Since then, prices have remained stable. Overall, rent has increased significantly over the five years.

units.title: Cause and effect
units.cando: Explain causes and results: lead to, result in, due to, have an effect on.

words.ex: Heavy rain caused flooding.
Lack of sleep can lead to poor concentration.
The changes resulted in fewer accidents.
The class was cancelled due to illness.
Rents rose. As a result, many students moved.
Exercise has a positive effect on mood.
Social media can contribute to stress.
Cost is a major factor in students’ choices.

pre.q: Lack of sleep can ___ poor concentration.
The flight was cancelled ___ bad weather.
Smoking ___ a negative effect on health.

pre.s: The new rules resulted {to} fewer accidents.

pre.q: Stress is a major ___ in poor exam performance.

notice.title: Paragraph: Why do students feel stressed?
notice.instr: Read the paragraph. Tap the words and phrases that show a cause or a result.
notice.text: Student stress has many causes. Part-time work is [[a major factor]], because it reduces time for study. Long working hours can [[lead to]] tiredness, which [[has a negative effect on]] concentration. [[Due to]] high rents, many students must work more. [[As a result]], they sleep less. Social media can also [[contribute to]] stress. Together, these problems often [[result in]] lower marks.
notice.after: Look at the small words in each phrase: lead to, result in, effect on. You’ll work out the patterns next.

discover.ctx: can lead to tiredness · often result in lower marks
discover.q: In ‘A leads to B’, which one happens first?
o: A is the cause; B is the result
B is the cause; A is the result
discover.hint: Long working hours → tiredness.
discover.insight: cause → lead to / result in / cause / contribute to → effect. (Careful: result from goes the other way: B results from A.)

discover.ctx: Due to high rents, many students must work more. · As a result, they sleep less.
discover.q: What comes after due to, and how is as a result used?
o: due to + noun phrase; As a result, + a new sentence
due to + subject + verb; as a result + noun
Both are followed by a noun
discover.hint: Is ‘high rents’ a noun or a clause?
discover.insight: due to / because of + noun (due to high rents). because + subject + verb. As a result, starts a new sentence.

discover.ctx: has a negative effect on concentration · contribute to stress
discover.q: Which preposition goes with effect?
discover.hint: Look at the text.
discover.insight: have an effect on (effect is a noun). affect is the verb: Stress affects sleep.

rule.title: Your word card
points: Cause → result: cause, lead to, result in, contribute to (one of several causes).
Reason: due to / because of + noun; because + subject + verb.
Linking sentences: As a result, … / Therefore, …
have an effect on (noun) / affect (verb); a major factor in.
rule.watch: <s>result to</s> → result in; <s>lead stress</s> → lead to stress; <s>due to it was late</s> → because it was late.

practice.q: The road was closed ___ an accident.
Exercise can have a positive effect ___ mental health.
Many students work long hours. ___, they have less time to study.
Social media can ___ how young people see themselves.
practice.why: affect = verb; effect = noun (have an effect on).

practice.a: Rising rents have led to longer working hours.

post.q: Heavy rain ___ flooding in many areas.
The event was postponed ___ the storm.
Noise can ___ a serious effect on sleep.

post.s: The new policy resulted {on} lower costs.

post.q: Air pollution can ___ to breathing problems.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences explaining the causes and effects of a problem you know (for example, traffic in your city, or stress at university). Use at least four cause-and-effect expressions.
produce.target: cause and effect language: cause, lead to, result in, contribute to, due to, as a result, have an effect on
checklist: I used the right preposition: lead to, result in, effect on.
After due to I used a noun phrase.
I used As a result, to start a sentence.
produce.model: Traffic in my city is a serious problem, mainly due to the lack of public transport. Long journeys lead to stress and tiredness. As a result, many workers arrive late. Car pollution also contributes to poor air quality, which has a negative effect on people’s health.

units.title: Talking about research and data
units.cando: Use key academic words for research: conduct a study, collect data, the findings indicate…

words.m: do research in a planned way
words.ex: We conducted a study with 300 students.
Data was collected through online surveys.
We analysed the data in Excel.
Interviews were the main research method.
The study identified three main problems.
The findings were published in 2024.
The results indicate a link between sleep and mood.

words.m: large or important enough to matter; in statistics, not just chance
words.ex: There was a significant difference between the groups.

pre.q: The researchers ___ a study with 300 participants.
Data was ___ through online surveys.
The findings ___ that sleep affects memory.

pre.s: We {analysis} the data using statistics software.

pre.q: There was a statistically ___ difference between the two groups.

notice.title: From a journal article abstract (invented example)
notice.instr: Read the abstract. Tap the research words and phrases: how the study was done and what it found.
notice.text: This study examined how part-time work affects university results. We [[conducted a survey]] of 420 undergraduate students and [[collected data]] on their working hours and grades. A mixed [[research method]] was used: the survey was followed by 20 interviews. We [[analysed the data]] using regression. The [[findings indicate]] that working more than 15 hours a week has a [[significant]] negative effect on grades. The interviews [[identified]] tiredness as the main problem.
notice.after: Which verbs go with study and data? How sure is indicate? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: conducted a survey · collected data · analysed the data
discover.q: Which verb does NOT go with ‘a study’ or ‘research’?
discover.hint: Think of make / do from the B1 unit.
discover.insight: We conduct / carry out / do research or a study. make research is a common error.

discover.ctx: The findings indicate that working more than 15 hours… has a negative effect.
discover.q: How sure is indicate?
o: It shows something is likely, but doesn’t prove it
It means the writer is guessing
discover.hint: Researchers are careful with their claims.
discover.insight: indicate / suggest = show (but not prove). Researchers rarely say prove. Stronger: demonstrate, show.

discover.ctx: a significant negative effect
discover.q: In research, significant usually means…
o: large enough to matter, or not just chance
discover.hint: It isn’t about being interesting.
discover.insight: significant = important or large enough to matter. Statistically significant = unlikely to be chance.

rule.title: Your word card
points: Doing research: conduct / carry out a study, collect / gather data, analyse data, use a research method.
Results: the findings (plural) indicate / suggest / show that…
identify a problem / a trend / a factor; a significant difference / effect / increase.
rule.watch: Data can take a singular or plural verb in academic writing (the data was / were collected). Choose one and be consistent.

practice.q: Researchers ___ the data to look for patterns.
practice.hint: It means ‘examined in detail’. Australian spelling: -yse.

practice.q: The results ___ that the new method is more effective.

practice.s: They {made} a study on student motivation.
practice.why: conduct / carry out / do a study

practice.q: Which phrase means ‘the results of a study’?

practice.a: The study identified three main factors.

practice.instr: Doing the research, or reporting the results?

post.q: We ___ research on climate anxiety in teenagers.
Data ___ over six months.
The ___ suggest that more research is needed.

post.why: You need the verb: identify → identified.

post.q: There was no ___ difference between men and women.

produce.task: Imagine you did a small study (for example, about students’ phone use). Write 3–4 sentences describing what you did and what you found. Use at least four research words from this unit.
produce.target: research vocabulary: conduct a study, collect/analyse data, method, identify, findings, indicate/suggest, significant
checklist: I used conduct / carry out (not make) with study or research.
I described the method and the findings.
I used indicate or suggest instead of prove.
produce.model: We conducted a small study on phone use among 50 first-year students. Data was collected through a short online survey and analysed in Excel. The findings indicate that students check their phones about 80 times a day. We also identified a significant link between phone use at night and tiredness in class.

units.title: Problems and solutions
units.cando: Discuss problems and solutions in essays: tackle an issue, pose a challenge, implement a policy.

words.ex: The city must tackle the problem of traffic.
Housing is a pressing issue for students.
Rising sea levels pose a threat to coastal towns.

words.m: have to deal with a difficulty
words.ex: Many graduates face the challenge of finding work.

words.m: do things to solve a problem
words.ex: The school took measures to reduce bullying.
The policy was implemented in 2024.
Public transport is an effective solution to congestion.

words.m: help people know about a problem
words.ex: The campaign raised awareness of mental health.

pre.q: Governments must ___ the problem of homelessness.
Rising sea levels ___ a serious threat to coastal cities.
The council plans to ___ a new policy to reduce traffic.

pre.s: The campaign aims to {rise} awareness of mental health.

pre.q: Recycling alone is not an ___ solution to plastic pollution.

notice.title: Essay paragraph: Traffic congestion
notice.instr: Read the paragraph. Tap the phrases about problems and solutions.
notice.text: Traffic congestion is [[a pressing issue]] in many large cities. It [[poses a challenge]] for workers and harms air quality. To [[tackle this problem]], governments should [[take measures]] such as improving public transport. Some cities have [[implemented a policy]] of charging drivers to enter the city centre, and this has proved to be [[an effective solution]]. Campaigns can also [[raise awareness]] of cheaper and healthier options, like cycling.
notice.after: Which verbs go with problem, challenge, policy and awareness? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: tackle this problem · address the issue
discover.q: What do ‘tackle a problem’ and ‘address an issue’ mean?
discover.hint: What should governments do about traffic?
discover.insight: tackle / address / deal with a problem or issue = make an effort to solve it.

discover.ctx: Traffic congestion poses a challenge.
discover.q: Which sentence is natural?
o: The government poses a challenge to solve it.
discover.hint: Who or what poses the challenge in the text?
discover.insight: A problem poses a challenge / threat / risk. People face a challenge.

discover.ctx: take measures · implemented a policy · raise awareness
discover.q: Which verb means ‘put a plan or policy into action’?
discover.hint: What did some cities do with the policy?
discover.insight: implement a policy / plan; take measures / steps; raise awareness of.

rule.title: Your word card
points: Problems: a pressing / serious issue; X poses a challenge / threat / risk; people face a challenge.
Action: tackle / address a problem; take measures / steps; implement a policy; raise awareness of.
Results: an effective solution; reduce the impact.
rule.watch: <s>rise awareness</s> → raise awareness (raise has an object; rise doesn’t).

practice.q: Many young people ___ the challenge of finding affordable housing.
practice.hint: People ___ a challenge; problems pose challenges.

practice.q: Schools should ___ awareness of online safety.

practice.s: Unemployment {makes} a serious challenge for young graduates.

practice.q: Which sentence is the most academic?
o: We need to do something about the problem.
Urgent measures must be taken to address the problem.
We should fix this thing quickly.
practice.hint: Look for collocations from this unit.

practice.a: The government must take urgent measures.

post.q: Universities need to ___ the issue of student wellbeing.
Cyber attacks ___ a growing threat to businesses.
The new policy was ___ in 2024.

post.s: The documentary helped to {rise} awareness of plastic pollution.

post.q: Housing costs are a ___ issue in Australian cities.

produce.task: Choose a problem in your city or country. Write 3–4 sentences: describe the problem and suggest solutions. Use at least four expressions from this unit.
produce.target: problem-solution collocations: tackle/address an issue, pose a challenge, take measures, implement a policy, raise awareness, an effective solution
checklist: A problem poses a challenge; people face it.
I used raise (not rise) awareness.
I suggested at least one solution.
produce.model: Air pollution is a pressing issue in my city, and it poses a serious threat to children’s health. To tackle this problem, the government should implement a policy of low-emission zones. It should also take measures to improve public transport. Finally, schools could raise awareness of the health risks.

units.title: Reporting verbs: how strong is the claim?
units.cando: Report sources accurately with verbs like suggest, argue, demonstrate and acknowledge.

words.ex: The trial demonstrated that the drug was safe.
The results suggest a possible link.
Early data indicate a small improvement.
Lee (2020) argued that fees should be lower.
Fischer (2021) contended that the effect was small.

words.m: say something is true (the writer may doubt it)
words.ex: Rossi (2020) claimed that games improve memory.
Several studies have questioned this view.

words.m: admit or accept a point, often a limitation
words.ex: The authors acknowledged that the sample was small.

pre.q: Lee (2022) ___ that social media harms sleep, but other studies disagree.
The experiment clearly ___ that the drug works.
Although she supports the approach, the writer ___ that it has some problems.
Which verb shows that the writer DOUBTS the source?

pre.instr: Type a verb that means ‘admitted’. It starts with a…
pre.q: The authors ___ that their findings may not apply to other countries.

notice.title: Literature review paragraph (invented sources)
notice.instr: Read the paragraph. Tap the verbs the writer uses to report what each source says.
notice.text: Research on homework is divided. Ahmed (2019) [[argued]] that homework improves achievement, and his large review [[demonstrated]] a clear link for older students. However, Fischer (2021) [[questioned]] this view and [[contended]] that homework mainly increases stress. Recent data [[suggest]] that the effect depends on age. Nguyen (2023) [[claimed]] that homework has no benefit at all, although she [[acknowledged]] that her sample was small.
notice.after: Each verb tells you how strong the source’s claim is and what the writer thinks of it. You’ll work out how next.

discover.ctx: Ahmed’s review demonstrated a clear link. · Recent data suggest that the effect depends on age.
discover.q: Which verb is stronger (more certain)?
discover.hint: Which one sounds like proof?
discover.insight: demonstrate / show = strong evidence. suggest / indicate = more careful (tentative).

discover.ctx: Nguyen (2023) claimed that homework has no benefit at all…
discover.q: Why might the writer choose claimed here?
o: To show doubt: the writer isn’t sure it’s true
discover.hint: Look at what follows: ‘her sample was small’.
discover.insight: claim often signals that the writer doubts the source. Your choice of reporting verb shows your stance.

discover.ctx: Fischer (2021) questioned this view and contended that… · she acknowledged that her sample was small.
discover.q: Which verb reports a source admitting a weakness?
discover.hint: Which one is about a limitation?
discover.insight: acknowledge = admit a limitation; question = doubt; contend / argue = put forward a position with reasons.

rule.title: Your word card
points: Strong: demonstrate, show, establish.
Position: argue, contend, state, note.
Tentative: suggest, indicate.
Doubt or disagreement: claim (the writer is unsure), question, challenge.
Admitting: acknowledge, concede.
rule.watch: Pattern: argue that…, suggest that… (not suggest to). In APA style, report a specific study in the past or present perfect: Ahmed (2019) argued / has argued…

practice.q: The data ___ that the policy may have reduced crime, but more research is needed.
Ali (2020) ___ that the sample was not representative, which limits the findings.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences reporting two or three sources on a topic you know (you can invent them). Choose reporting verbs that show how strong each claim is and what you think of it.
produce.target: reporting verbs and stance: demonstrate, show, suggest, indicate, argue, contend, claim, question, acknowledge
checklist: I chose strong verbs only for strong evidence.
I used claim or question to show doubt.
I used verb + that (argued that…).
produce.model: Ahmed (2019) demonstrated a clear link between sleep and exam results in a study of 2,000 students. Fischer (2021) argued that the link is weaker for older students. However, Lopez (2022) claimed that sleep has no effect at all, although she acknowledged that her sample was very small.

units.title: Evaluating evidence
units.cando: Judge sources and evidence with collocations like compelling evidence and widely accepted.

words.ex: There is compelling evidence that smoking causes cancer.
There is only limited evidence for this diet.

words.m: studies that disagree with each other
words.ex: The evidence on coffee is conflicting.
The large sample produced robust findings.
A growing body of research links exercise and mood.
The theory is now widely accepted.
The study sheds light on how children learn.
New data called the old theory into question.

notice.title: Literature review paragraph
notice.instr: Read the paragraph. Tap the phrases the writer uses to judge the evidence.
notice.text: There is [[a growing body of research]] on the benefits of being bilingual. Early studies provided [[compelling evidence]] that bilingual children have better attention control, and this view became [[widely accepted]]. However, more recent studies have [[called into question]] these results, and there is now [[conflicting evidence]]. Some large studies have produced [[robust findings]] of no difference. More research is needed to [[shed light on]] when, and for whom, being bilingual helps. In short, the evidence for broad benefits is [[limited]].
notice.after: Some phrases make the evidence sound strong, others weak or unclear. You’ll sort them out next.

discover.ctx: compelling evidence · conflicting evidence · limited evidence
discover.q: Which adjective means that different studies disagree?
discover.hint: Two studies, two different results.
discover.insight: compelling / strong / robust = convincing; limited / weak = not enough; conflicting / mixed = studies disagree.

discover.ctx: this view became widely accepted · a growing body of research
discover.q: Widely accepted means…
discover.hint: Widely = by many people.
discover.insight: widely accepted / held / used = by many people. a growing body of research / evidence = more and more studies.

discover.ctx: studies have called into question these results · research is needed to shed light on…
discover.q: Which phrase means ‘make people doubt’?
discover.hint: Shed light = make clearer.
discover.insight: call into question = cause doubt about; shed light on = help explain.

rule.title: Your word card
points: Strong: compelling / robust / convincing evidence; findings are widely accepted.
Weak or unclear: limited / weak / anecdotal evidence; conflicting / mixed evidence.
Change: a growing body of research; new studies call into question or shed light on…
Evidence is uncountable: some evidence, a piece of evidence (not evidences).

practice.q: Studies have found opposite results, so the evidence is ___.
The study was very small, so the evidence is ___.

practice.s: The court heard many {evidences} against him.
practice.why: Evidence is uncountable: many pieces of evidence / a lot of evidence.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences evaluating the evidence on a topic you know (for example, coffee and health, or homework). Use at least four phrases from this unit.
produce.target: collocations for evaluating evidence: compelling/limited/conflicting evidence, a growing body of research, widely accepted, call into question, shed light on
checklist: I used evidence as uncountable (no -s).
I showed how strong the evidence is.
I used at least four phrases from the word card.
produce.model: There is a growing body of research on coffee and health. Several large studies provide compelling evidence that moderate coffee drinking is safe for most adults. However, the evidence on pregnant women is limited, and some smaller studies have produced conflicting results. Further research may shed light on why people react differently to caffeine.
